title: Metaleorganic framework-mediated strategy for enhanced methane production on copper nanoparticles in electrochemical CO2 reduction
abstract: Conversion of carbon dioxide (CO2) to useful chemicals is considered a potential solution to resolve the climate threat. In this study, a facile metal-organic framework (MOF)-mediated strategy to obtain an efficient electrocatalyst for the synthesis of methane (CH4) is suggested. Cu-based MOF-74 was chosen as the precursor, which was electrochemically reduced to obtain Cu nanoparticles (NPs). The porous structure of the MOF serves as a template for the synthesis of isolated Cu NP clusters with high catalytic activities and high efficiencies for the CH4 production in the electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction. The MOF-derived Cu NPs demonstrate high Faradaic efficiency (>50%) for the CH4 production with suppressed C2 production, and 2.3-fold higher methanation activity at 1.3 V (vs. RHE) compared to the commercial Cu NPs. © 2019 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Electrochemical carbon dioxide reduction reaction (CO2RR) has attracted much attention as a means to mitigate the amount of CO2 in the atmosphere and produce renewable and clean energy via the capture and conversion of CO2 to value-added fuels and chemicals [1e4]. For the practical application of this technique, various catalyst materials that can efficiently produce the desired chemicals have been explored. For instance, Cu has been vastly studied as an electrocatalyst for its ability to produce various forms of hydrocarbons during the CO2RR [5e7]. The application of Cu as a CO2RR electrocatalyst was first reported by Hori et al., who discovered that at adequately negative potentials, hydrocarbons such as methane (CH4) and ethylene (C2H4) are produced in sufficient amounts on Cu

electrodes [5,6,8]. Nonetheless, for more practical reasons, strategies to suppress the diversity of products generated from the CO2RR on Cu electrodes and increase the selectivity towards a certain product have been developed [9e13].
Among the CO2RR products, carbon monoxide, formate, and ethylene are generally considered to be valuable since the technoeconomic analyses report that the cost of synthesizing these chemicals via CO2 electrolysis is comparable to the current market value [14,15]. Methane, on the other hand, is less valuable regarding the energy input and cannot be used for the direct conversion into other chemicals. Despite so, methane, which is the main component of natural gas, is used in high abundance (21.4% of the total primary energy sources) [16] and its usefulness has recently been re-emphasized since methane could potentially be efficiently recycled from CO2 and used within the current energy infrastructure [17,18]. In the renewable energy industries, methane is also considered a potential solar fuel especially because it could be stored and manipulated more conveniently than H2 [19,20]. Therefore, selective production of methane via renewable methods is desired. The use of nanostructured Cu-based electrodes has emerged as an efficient strategy for the selective production of methane in the CO2RR. This is because multi-electron transfers in electrochemical reactions are highly influenced by the particle size
of the electrode material [11,21]. Moreover, recent studies have suggested that isolated Cu atoms show higher efficiency for the CH4 production compared to Cu alloys [21,22]. Such findings led to the synthesis of small Cu particles, which exhibited higher Faradaic efficiency (FE) for the CH4 production and suppressed ethylene gas formation, as compared to Cu foil [11]. However, Cu nanoparticles (NPs) tend to easily agglomerate, and a high loading of Cu NPs often leads to an undesired enhancement in FE for C2 and C3 products due to the enhanced CeC coupling reactions [22,23]. Therefore, a synthetic strategy to fabricate Cu-based electrocatalysts that are not only nanosized but also sufficiently isolated is required to promote CH4 production on Cu.
Recently, metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) have caught attention as promising candidates for gas capture and as CO2 conversion catalysts. MOFs are well-known for their unique properties such as high surface areas due to their high porosities and structural or chemical tenability [24e31]. Although they can be easily fabricated and modified using different chemicals and ligands [32e34], their applications to the electrochemical CO2RR has been limited due to their low thermodynamic stabilities under reduction potentials [35e37]. Therefore, additional processes are generally required to convert MOFs into functionalized materials and metal or metal oxide NPs that possess both the structural properties of MOFs and electrochemical stabilities [35e37].
In this work, we used Cu-based MOF (MOF-74) as the precursor of highly isolated Cu NPs clusters to achieve enhanced CH4 production in the CO2RR. MOF-74 was chosen because of its lowdimensional structure, which could prevent agglomeration of the reduced Cu clusters [38]. We expected that the electroreduction of Cu-MOF-74 would lead to the formation of highly isolated Cu NP clusters, which could promote the methane production activity. As hypothesized, the Cu NPs derived from Cu-MOF-74 (m-Cu NP), comprised aligned and isolated Cu NP clusters and exhibited enhanced activity and selectivity towards the CH4 production during the CO2RR compared to commercial Cu NPs (c-Cu NPs).

sections.heading: 2.1. Materials and chemicals
sections.text: Cu nanopowder (particle size¼ 20e30 nm, 99.5% trace metal basis), copper(II) nitrate trihydrate (Cu(NO3)2$3H2O, 99e104%), and potassium carbonate (ACS reagent, 99%) were purchased from Sigma Aldrich. Nafion® D-520 dispersion (5% w/w in water and 1- propanol, >1.00 meq/g exchange capacity) and glassy carbon plate (1mm (0.04 in) thick, type 1) were purchased fromAlfa Aesar. 2,5-dihydroxyterephthalic acid (H4DOBDC, >98.0%) and 1,3,5- benzenetricarboxylic acid (H3BTC, >98.0%) were purchased from TCI. N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF, >98.80%), methanol (HPLC, 99.9%) and ethanol (HPLC, 99.9%) were purchased from Daejung Chemicals. 2-propanol was obtained from Samchun Chemicals. All reagents were used without further purification.

sections.heading: 2.2. Synthesis of Cu-MOF-74 and MOF-derived Cu NPs
sections.text:
Cu-MOF-74 was synthesized according to the procedure described elsewhere [25,39]. Typically, 2.5 g of H4DOBDC (1.1mmol) and 0.59 g of Cu(NO3)2$3H2O (2.4mmol) were dissolved in 25mL of 20:1 (v/v) solution of DMF and 2-propanol in a 30mL vial. Then, the vial was placed in an oven at 80 C for 24 h. After synthesis, the reddish powders were cooled to room temperature and washed three times with DMF and methanol, respectively. Finally, the MOFs were activated at 60 C under vacuum for 12 h.
To obtain Cu NPs from Cu-MOF-74, the synthesized Cu-MOF-74 was first made into a slurry with Nafion in a specific weight ratio
(95:5), which was subsequently dispersed in ethanol by hand milling. Next, the Cu-MOF-74 suspension was spin coated on a glassy carbon (active area¼ 1 cm2) electrode. In all experiments, 0.1M potassium bicarbonate (KHCO3) was used as the electrolyte. Cu-MOF-74 was electrochemically reduced using a standard threeelectrode setup composed of the spin-coated Cu-MOF-74/glassy carbon plate as the working electrode, platinum counter electrode, and Ag/AgCl reference electrode. Finally, Cu NPs were derived from Cu-MOF-74 by linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) at a scan rate of 20mV/s from 0 to 1.4 V (vs. RHE) and chronoamperometry (CA) at 1.4 V (vs. RHE) for 30min.

sections.heading: 2.3. Material characterization
sections.text: The morphologies of the c-Cu NPs and m-Cu NPs were studied by variable-pressure field-emission scanning electron microscopy (VP-FESEM, SUPRA55VP, Carl Zeiss) and field-emission transmission electron microscopy (FE-TEM, JEM-2100F, JEOL). The elemental mapping of Cu-MOF-74, before and after electroreduction, was performing using scanning TEM (STEM) energydispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS, X-MAS, Oxford instruments), and the crystal structures were analyzed by X-ray diffraction (XRD, X'pert PRO MPD, Malvern PANalytical).

sections.heading: 2.4. Electrochemical analysis
sections.text:
For all electrochemical measurements, a multipotentiostat (VMP3, BioLogic) was used. A standard three-electrode cell composed of working electrode, Pt counter electrode, and Ag/AgCl reference electrode was used. 0.1M potassium bicarbonate (KHCO3) was chosen as the electrolyte in order to enhance CH4 selectivity [40]. CO2 was delivered into the electrolysis cell at a flow rate of 5 standard cubic centimeters per minute (sccm). Working electrodes were all freshly prepared prior to each experiment, and LSV curves were used to test the repeatability of the fabricated electrodes.
Online gas chromatography (GC) was used to analyze the gaseous products formed at the cathode. During the constantpotential electrolysis, the electrolyte was purged with CO2 gas at a flow rate of 5 sccm, controlled with amass flow controller (Brooks Instrument, 5850E Series). The gaseous products such as H2, CO, CH4, or C2H4 were separated using a stainless steel column (1.8m 0.3 cm) packed with 80/100 Molecular Sieve 5 A (Restek® PLOT) and analyzed every 23min using a micro thermal conductivity detector (mTCD). After the electrolysis, the liquid products were collected and analyzed by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC, 1260 Infinity II, Agilent Technologies) with a SUGAR SH1101 (Shodex) column. Sulfuric acid (1mM) was used as the eluent, and the samples (20 mL) were automatically injected into the column using an autosampler. The temperature of the column was maintained at 75 C, and the detector used was a refractive index detector (RID).

sections.heading: 3. Results and discussion
sections.text:
Cu-MOF-74 was synthesized according to a well-known procedure [38,39] using Cu(NO3)2$3H2O as the Cu precursor and H4DOBDC as an organic linker [39]. The MOF-74 structure is composed of one-dimensional (1D) rods of inorganic metal precursor and organic linkers, wherein each metal ion is coordinated to carboxyl and hydroxyl groups, and a coordinating ligand (Fig. 1). Before the preparation of m-Cu NPs, the Cu-MOF-74 precursor was washed and activated to remove the residual reactants and empty cavities. Because the synthesized Cu-MOF-74 sample was comprised of rods with a honeycomb-like structure, we
hypothesized that it should be possible to obtain isolated Cu NP clusters from Cu-MOF-74 by electrochemically reducing it.
Themorphology of the as-synthesized Cu-MOF-74was analyzed by SEM and TEM (Fig. 2). The simulation-derived crystal structure (CCDC number: 901474) of Cu-MOF-74 [39] is shown in Fig. 2a. Because the metal ions and linkers in MOF-74 are ordered in a 1D hexagonal shape, the synthesized Cu-MOF-74 sample exhibits a typical rod-shaped morphology corresponding to the MOF-74 structure, as shown in Fig. 2b. The high-magnification SEM and
TEM images (Fig. 2cee) of Cu-MOF-74 reveal rod-shaped structures with diameters of ~2 mm and lengths in tens of micrometers. In addition, the sample exhibits the characteristic XRD peaks at 6.79467 and 11.7826 (Fig. 2f), indicating the presence of pores with sizes 14.8722 Å; the XRD result agrees well with the theoretical value for the MOF-74 structure [29,39]. These results show that Cu ions are arranged regularly in the highly crystalline MOF structure, from which we expected that the resulting electrocatalyst will maintain its original structure to a certain degree even

To synthesize m-Cu NPs, Cu-MOF-74 was coated on a glassy carbon electrode and electrochemically reduced by LSV, followed by CA at 1.4 V (vs. RHE). The schematic diagram of Cu NP preparation from Cu-MOF-74 is given in Fig. 1. The SEM image of the CuMOF-74 on glassy carbon electrode before reduction presented in Fig. 3a shows rod-shapedMOF particles. In contrast, the SEM image of the reduced sample (Fig. 3b) reveals the formation of clusters consisting of several particles with 30e50 nm in sizes. Thus, the SEM images obtained before and after the electroreduction process clearly show the difference in the MOF morphology, indicating the formation of nanoparticles via the electrochemical reduction of Cu ions in the MOF structure. To confirm the presence of elemental constituents of the MOF and MOF-derived Cu NPs, we performed TEM, STEM and EDS elemental mapping on Cu-MOF-74 before and after electroreduction (Fig. 3cee). Cu-MOF-74 was mainly composed of Cu, C, and O, which constitute the inorganic and organic components of the MOFs (Fig. 3c). After the electroreduction of Cu-MOF-74, NPs with sizes of 30e50 nmwere found to be distributed along the original MOF structure (Fig. 3d). As observed, the NPs were mainly composed of Cu, and the intensities of C and O peaks diminished. This result confirms the formation of Cu NPs via the removal of organic components from the Cu-MOF-74 framework during the electroreduction process. It should be also noted that the synthesized Cu NPs possess the inherent structure of Cu-MOF-74. The XRD patterns recorded before and after the electroreduction process confirm that the m-Cu NPs were derived from Cu-MOF-74 (Fig. 3e); the diffraction pattern of the as-synthesized Cu-MOF-74 sample (blue) matched well with the theoretical and
experimental patterns, as reported elsewhere [38,39,41]. After the electroreduction (red), the main peaks of the porous MOF structure were dramatically suppressed, while the strong peaks corresponding to metallic Cu were newly observed at 43.473 (JCPDS reference code 00-001-1241). In addition, minor CuO peaks (JCPDS reference code: 00-001-1117) were detected, which were attributed to the surface oxidation of Cu NPs during sample preparation for the powder XRD (PXRD) analysis. The residual MOF-74 peaks due to the unreacted inner surface of Cu-MOF-74 on the glassy carbon electrode were also detected. Moreover, the reduced metallic Cu phase of m-Cu NPs was observed by HRTEM and the selected area electron diffraction (Fig. 3f), which corresponds to the PXRD analysis.
To evaluate the electrocatalytic performance of the m-Cu NPs, we measured the electrochemical activity and analyzed the CO2RR products under various conditions. The m-Cu NPs and c-Cu NPs on glassy carbon plate were assembled as cathodes in flow cells containing 0.1M KHCO3 aqueous solution, Pt foil, and Ag/AgCl electrode as the electrolyte, the counter and the reference electrodes, respectively. Fig. 4a shows the LSV curves of m-CuNPs and c-Cu NPs obtained from 0.3 V to 1.4 V vs. RHE at a scan rate of 20mV/s. As observed, the m-Cu NPs exhibit a current density of 10.9mA/cm2 at 1.4 V (vs. RHE), which is 2.4 times higher than that of c-Cu NPs. Moreover, product analysis performed under various applied potentials via online GC and ex-situ HPLC revealed that the CO2RR selectivity of the m-Cu NPs is distinctly different from that of the cCu NPs (Fig. 4b and c). During the reduction reaction, the FE for CH4 reached approximately 50%, while that for C2H4 maintained <10% at 1.3 V (vs. RHE). In contrast, the c-Cu NP electrode exhibited 28.7% and 29.5% for the FEs for the CH4 and C2H4 formations,

To compare the overall activity and selectivity of the different Cu NPs, the FEs for C1 and C2 products were plotted as a function of the applied potentials (Fig. 5a). As observed, at potentials lower

At 1.3 V vs. RHE, where methanation activity was the highest, partial current densities towards the CH4 production on m-Cu NPs were calculated to be 2.3-times those of the c-Cu NPs (Fig. 5a, red axis). Works from several different groups have reported that the selectivity of the methanation reaction on copper nanoparticles is closely related to the extent of aggregation of the particles at nanoscales [11,22,42]. For instance, Manthiaram, et al. suggested that isolated nanoparticles tend to expose catalytic sites more adequate for the methanation reaction, but such sites are lost as they form aggregates [21]. Nie et al. proposed that the formation of methane and ethylene both share similar reaction paths on Cu (111), but whether the CH2* intermediate can undergo a nonelectrochemical dimerization influences the selectivity between the two products [43]. In a separate work, these speculations were confirmed experimentally by isolating Cu nanoclusters onto defect sites in the graphene sheet, which enhanced the production rate and selectivity toward CH4 with a strong suppression of C-C coupling reaction pathway [44]. We have confirmed our speculation by investigating the morphologies of the c-Cu NP andm-Cu NP electrodes by SEM (Fig. 5b and c); more intense particle agglomeration was observed in the c-Cu NP sample. In contrast, physically separated Cu NPs were observed on the surface of the m-Cu NP electrode. Such physical isolation of the constituent nanoparticles of m-Cu NP electrodes, which enhances the product selectivity towards methane formation, is perhaps maintained from the original MOF structure.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
In this study, we fabricated Cu NPs via a facile method based on MOFs to exploit their structural advantages in electrochemical CO2 reduction. We expected that the inherent structure of MOF would influence the particle size of the formed NPs, and therefore electrochemically reduced Cu-based MOF-74. The resulting MOFderived Cu NPs were found to be less aggregated and demonstrated outstanding electrocatalytic performances with high activity and selectivity for C1 products. The high selectivity towards the CH4 formation could be attributed to the suppression of CeC coupling (for C2 product formation) due to the isolated NP clusters. Moreover, the Cu NPs derived from MOFs exhibited 2.3-fold higher methanation activity and enhanced FE (>50%) for CH4 than commercial Cu NPs.
